title.en: Sweet words with a sharp edge

text.en: Have you ever been praised so much that you felt you were the best in the world, and then something went wrong? This short poem by the French poet Jean de La Fontaine is about a clever fox, a proud raven and a piece of food. It takes only four stanzas to teach a lesson about pride and flattery.

Ravens are large black birds, and their voice is a rough croak, not a song. The book says even ravens croak, as frogs do. In stories, the fox is usually shown as the cunning animal. Keep that in mind as you meet the fox in this poem.
A raven is sitting on the branch of a tree, holding a small piece of food in his beak. The fox, whose name is Reynard, looks up at him hungrily. The fox would go far to get that food, so he does not ask for it. He flatters the raven instead. He calls the raven a handsome bird, praises his feathers and says that if he would only sing, the birds of the woods would crown him their king.
The raven does not see that the fox is joking. He forgets that his voice is only a croak. Filled with foolish pride, he opens his beak to sing, and the food drops down to the fox. So in the poem pride makes the raven forget the truth about himself, and that is the mistake.
The fox laughs and tells the raven to ignore sweet words that only make you feel good. He adds that pride is unwise and that the raven has just got a surprising lesson. This is the moral of the fable. The moral is: do not be fooled by flattery, and do not be too proud of yourself.
Perched means sat on something, here on a branch. A limb is a branch of a tree. A morsel is a small piece of food. To seek is to look for something. Eyed means looked at with interest. Pride here means feeling that you are better than others. The woods are a small forest area with similar trees. Opposites from the book include flew and perched, remembered and forgot, wise and foolish, humility and pride, cried and laughed, notice and ignore, dim and glow.
Rhyming words end with the same sound. In stanza 1 limb rhymes with him, and in stanza 4 know rhymes with glow. Alliteration is the repetition of the same consonant sound at the start of nearby words, such as big beak, where both begin with the b sound. The book asks you to find another example in stanza 2. Reading the lines aloud helps you hear the repeated sound. Poets use rhyme and alliteration to make a poem musical and easy to remember.
You can narrate the poem as a story. A good start is: this is a story about a clever fox named Reynard and Mr Raven, and then you say what happened one day. You can give it a different ending, for example a raven who keeps the food and laughs at the fox. You can also write it as a conversation. Remember the raven holds food in his beak, so he only shows actions like nodding and does not speak. Stick puppets and origami birds are a fun way to enact the poem in class.

problem.en: Write one word from the poem to complete the analogy: Fox is to clever as Raven is to ____.

text.en: Notice the fox is described as clever or cunning.

why.en: The analogy compares the fox with the raven.

text.en: The raven fell for flattery, so the word is foolish, which the poem uses for his pride.

why.en: The poem says the raven opened his beak in foolish pride.

problem.en: Find the opposites: perched, forgot, foolish, pride.

text.en: Pair each word with a meaning on the other side.

why.en: Perched means sat, so the opposite is flew; forgot is the opposite of remembered.

text.en: Foolish is opposite to wise, and pride is opposite to humility.

why.en: Humility means not thinking too highly of yourself.

prompt.en: Explain what the raven learned in the poem and how you would handle too much praise.

requiredIdeas.en: The raven opened his beak because of the fox praise and lost his food.
Flattery is sweet words meant to get something.
A wise person stays calm and thinks before acting on praise.
Pride makes us forget our weaknesses.

commonMisconceptions.en: The fox was kind and wanted to make the raven king.
The raven was clever and tricked the fox.

points.en: The Raven and the Fox is a four-stanza poem by Jean de La Fontaine.
The fox flatters the raven so that he will sing and drop his food.
Pride made the raven forget that his voice was only a croak.
The moral is to ignore flattery and not be too proud.
Alliteration repeats beginning consonant sounds; rhyming words end with the same sound.
